COLDWAR_SOV_ns_shock_workers: The Stakhanovites of the 1930s smashed every norm and became heroes of the nation. Trapeznikov's circle wants that spirit back: shock brigades, red banners on the shop floor and public honour for those who overfulfil the plan. The trade unions grumble about speed-ups and raised norms, but the Neo-Stalinists believe socialist emulation can achieve what Kosygin's bonuses never did.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_cadres_decide_everything: In May 1935 Stalin told the graduates of the Red Army academies that cadres decide everything. The Neo-Stalinist platform takes the slogan literally: the nomenklatura is to be rebuilt as a disciplined, ideologically reliable corps, promoted for loyalty and results rather than seniority. The Central Committee apparatus, long used to Brezhnev's comfortable stability of cadres, is promised a firmer hand and a renewed sense of mission.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_the_new_purge: Corruption, nepotism and quiet private dealing have spread through the apparatus since Khrushchev's fall. The Neo-Stalinists answer with the oldest remedy they know: a purge of the ranks, carried out by the organs of state security and justified in the language of revolutionary vigilance. Thieves and careerists will fall, but so will many who merely backed the wrong patron, and the whole party will learn once more what fear means.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_the_patriotic_spirit: In May 1970 the country marked twenty-five years since the victory over fascism, and the memory of the Great Patriotic War remains the deepest source of Soviet legitimacy. The platform places the war, and the Generalissimo who led it, back at the centre of public life: new memorials, military-patriotic education in every school and a cult of sacrifice that binds the young to the generation of 1941.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_the_closed_economy: Western credits, Fiat licences and grain deals have made the Union dependent on its rivals, or so the Neo-Stalinists argue. Their answer is autarky: foreign trade reduced to what is strictly necessary, contacts with capitalist firms placed under suspicion and the economy organised to survive any embargo the imperialists might impose. Self-reliance has a price in technology and comfort, but it removes a lever the West could one day pull.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_collective_farms_tightene: Private plots and market sales have crept back into the countryside, and many kolkhozy survive only on state subsidies. The platform orders a return to discipline: tighter control over private livestock, firm delivery quotas and larger, consolidated farms run by reliable chairmen. Output may rise in the granaries, but the collective farmers will remember who took away the little freedom they had won since 1953.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_reconcile_with_mao: The clashes on Damansky Island in March 1969 brought the Soviet Union and China to the brink of war. Yet Mao has always despised Khrushchev's revisionism far more than Stalin's legacy, and a Moscow that rehabilitates Stalin might find an unexpected listener in Beijing. The platform proposes to offer the Chinese comrades a common return to the pure line, if they are willing to take it.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_the_iron_curtain_reinforc: Western radio, tourists, jazz records and smuggled jeans corrupt Soviet youth more effectively than any army could. The Neo-Stalinists want the frontier sealed once more: the jamming of the Voice of America and Radio Liberty is intensified, contacts with foreigners are restricted and cultural exchanges are cut back to the bare minimum. Trade with the West will suffer, but the ideological frontier of the Union will finally be secure.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_the_leadership_question: The Neo-Stalinist platform has always been divided on one point: should the restoration produce a new supreme leader, or must power remain with the collective Politburo? Some in Trapeznikov's circle dream of a new Vozhd who stands above the apparatus as Stalin did, while others fear another reign of terror that would devour its own creators. The movement must decide which path the restoration will take.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_a_new_vozhd: The decision is made: the Union will once again have a Vozhd. The General Secretary is elevated above the Politburo, his portraits fill the squares and his word becomes the final authority in party and state. Supporters call it the restoration of Leninist order; critics whisper that the country has seen all this before, and remember how it ended for the delegates of the Congress of Victors in 1934.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_collective_stalinism: Rather than create another Vozhd, the leadership chooses Stalinism without Stalin. The cult of the late Generalissimo is restored and many of his methods return, but power remains shared within the Politburo, where no single man can turn the organs against his colleagues. The nomenklatura welcomes a system that offers discipline from above and security for those who already sit at the top.
COLDWAR_SOV_ns_the_second_industrialisat: Stalin's first industrialisation turned a peasant land into a great power within a decade. The Neo-Stalinists now promise a second one: new giants such as the Kama truck works, power stations on the Siberian rivers and whole industrial cities built from scratch in the taiga. Mobilisation, central direction and sacrifice are once again to drive the Soviet economy forward, this time towards the twenty-first century.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_the_leader_state: Alexander Shelepin, the Iron Shurik who once led both the Komsomol and the KGB, has finally taken power together with his network of former Komsomol functionaries. The comfortable collective rule of the Brezhnev years is over. In its place stands a leader state, built on personal loyalty, youthful energy and a security apparatus that answers to one man rather than to the Politburo.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_the_vozhd_principle: Shelepin's followers do not hide what they want: a single leader whose authority rests on personal will rather than on the consensus of ageing Politburo members. The principle of the Vozhd is proclaimed openly, and the apparatus is told that loyalty to the leader is loyalty to the revolution itself. Few dare to ask aloud where this road led the last time it was travelled.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_the_youth_vanguard: The Komsomol, with more than twenty million members, is the largest reservoir of energy in the Union, and Shelepin knows it better than anyone. Its brigades are to become the vanguard of the new order, sent to the great construction sites, to the factories and to the border regions. The young are promised responsibility and rapid advancement in return for unconditional commitment.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_the_pillar: Every leader state needs a foundation, and Shelepin's advisers are divided on which one to choose. Some want to build the regime on the organs of state security, which Shelepin and Semichastny once commanded. Others want to rest it on the permanent mobilisation of the masses through the Komsomol and great national campaigns. The choice will define the character of the new order.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_the_security_state: The KGB was Shelepin's springboard to power, and it will now be his main pillar. Its directorates are expanded, its informers multiplied and its authority over party members restored to levels unseen since 1953. Every foreign influence and every whisper of dissent is to be detected early, and the Chekists become the guardians not only of the state but of the leader himself.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_the_informers: A security state rests on information, and information comes from people. A vast network of informers is recruited in factories, institutes, dormitories and housing blocks, many of them from the ranks of the Komsomol. Foreign intelligence services find it ever harder to operate, but trust between colleagues, neighbours and friends begins to wither, and the atmosphere in the country grows colder.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_mass_mobilisation: Rather than relying on the secret police, the regime builds its power on the masses. Rallies, voluntary labour Saturdays, people's patrol squads and endless campaigns keep society in permanent motion. The Komsomol Vanguard presents itself as the movement of a young and fighting generation, and anyone who stands aside quickly learns that indifference is also a political statement.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_the_great_campaigns: In the spirit of the Virgin Lands and the great Komsomol construction projects, the regime launches a new series of national campaigns. Tens of thousands of young volunteers are sent to the taiga, the steppe and the Far North to lay railways, raise dams and found new towns. The work is hard and the living conditions harsh, but the campaigns give the regime both results and legitimacy.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_purge_the_old_men: The Politburo of 1970 is a council of elderly men, many of whom have held high office since Stalin's days. Shelepin's young cadres now push them aside: pensions, honourable retirements and, where needed, humiliating dismissals clear the way for a new generation. The principle of stability of cadres that protected the old guard under Brezhnev is abandoned, and the whole apparatus trembles.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_construction_battalions: The Soviet Army already maintains construction battalions, but the new regime turns them, together with the Komsomol brigades, into a permanent labour force for the great projects. Roads, railways, pipelines and bridges are pushed into the remote regions of Siberia and the Far East at a pace no ordinary ministry could achieve. Discipline replaces wages as the main motivation.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_discipline_in_the_factori: Absenteeism, drinking at work and idle hours have become part of everyday life in Soviet industry. The new regime declares war on slackness: inspection teams patrol the factories, latecomers are named and shamed, and managers are held personally responsible for labour discipline. Productivity rises, but the trade unions lose what little ability they had to protect the workers they represent.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_the_iron_fist_abroad: The Brezhnev Doctrine already claims the right to intervene wherever socialism is threatened. Shelepin's regime goes further, promising its allies a firmer hand and its enemies a harder line from the Elbe to the Ussuri. Military aid to revolutionary movements grows, Soviet forces are placed on higher readiness, and the world is reminded that the young generation in Moscow does not fear confrontation.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_the_eastern_opening: Ideology has divided Moscow and Beijing for a decade, but two leader states may understand each other better than two parties ever did. Without abandoning Soviet interests, the regime signals to Mao that a pragmatic understanding is possible, building on the talks Kosygin and Zhou Enlai held at Beijing airport in September 1969. Whether China takes the outstretched hand is up to Beijing.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_the_succession: A regime built around one man has no ready answer to the question of what comes after him. Shelepin's circle must decide whether to designate an heir from among the loyal Komsomol cadres or to let power return to the party, where it lay before the leader state was proclaimed. The choice will decide whether the system survives its founder.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_heir_semichastny: Vladimir Semichastny succeeded Shelepin both as head of the Komsomol and as chairman of the KGB, and he has followed his mentor ever since. Brezhnev exiled him to a minor post in Kiev in 1967, but under the leader state he has returned to the centre. Naming him heir ensures that the security organs will stand behind the succession, and that Shelepin's line will continue.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_return_to_the_party: The age of the leader state draws to a close. Rather than handing power to a designated heir, the Komsomol Vanguard returns authority to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and its Central Committee. A plenum will decide the future course, and the comrades who survived the years of mobilisation must once again find a common line.
COLDWAR_SOV_kv_the_vanguard_state: The vanguard state has become an established order. The Komsomol generation now holds the key posts in party, state and security apparatus, and a young, disciplined elite governs a society trained in permanent mobilisation. Admirers see a socialism that has rediscovered its fighting energy; critics see a garrison state run by the former youth league. Either way, the Union has changed for good.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_the_systems_men_rule: Dzhermen Gvishiani, Kosygin's son-in-law and deputy chairman of the State Committee for Science and Technology, has long argued that the Union must be run like one great system. Now the systems men hold power: economists, cyberneticians and managers who speak the language of efficiency rather than ideology. Their rule is authoritarian and technocratic, but it looks westwards for methods and partners.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_the_iiasa_partnership: Together with McGeorge Bundy, Gvishiani has been negotiating an international institute where Soviet and American scientists could jointly study the problems of modern industrial societies. At Laxenburg near Vienna, the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis is set to become a bridge between East and West. For the Directorate it is a window on Western management science and a symbol of its new course.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_the_managerial_revolution: Party secretaries still meddle in every decision of every factory, and the nomenklatura confuses loyalty with competence. The Directorate puts an end to this: enterprise directors receive real authority, professional managers are trained on the model of Western business schools and promotion depends on measurable results. The old party apparatus watches with alarm as its grip on the economy slips away.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_the_form: The systems men agree on what they reject, but not on what they want to build. One faction envisions a technocratic state in which scientific institutes and planning bodies govern through models and data. The other dreams of a corporate union in which large industrial associations operate like Western corporations, open to foreign capital and trade. The Directorate must now choose its shape.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_the_technocratic_state: The Directorate chooses the path of the technocratic state. Ministries are reorganised according to systems analysis, planning bodies are staffed with mathematicians and engineers, and decisions are justified by models instead of quotations from Lenin. The state becomes more efficient and more powerful, but also more distant from the people it governs and more dependent on a small, closed elite of experts.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_the_corporate_union: The Directorate chooses the corporate path. Large industrial associations are transformed into semi-independent corporations that negotiate with foreign partners, raise credit abroad and compete for markets. Western banks and firms are invited to invest, and Soviet enterprises begin to resemble Fiat or Siemens more than a department of a ministry. Efficiency grows, and so does the foreign debt.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_western_licences: The giant car plant at Togliatti, agreed with Fiat in 1966, showed how quickly Western licences can close a technological gap. The Directorate makes this the rule rather than the exception: licences for production lines, electronics and chemical processes are purchased systematically, and Soviet engineers are sent abroad to learn. Critics warn of dependency, but the systems men see no shame in learning from the best.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_the_computer_ministry: Viktor Glushkov's plan for a nationwide automated management system, OGAS, was shelved by the old leadership, which feared what transparent data might reveal. The Directorate revives it under a dedicated ministry for computer technology. New microelectronics plants are built, the Ryad series of computers is expanded and a network linking the planning bodies becomes the backbone of a modern state.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_rationalise_the_army: The Soviet Armed Forces swallow a huge share of the nation's resources, yet nobody can say exactly how much security they produce. The Directorate applies systems analysis to defence: redundant divisions are disbanded, procurement is subjected to cost-effectiveness calculations and the bloated officer corps is reduced. The General Staff protests bitterly, but the systems men believe a smaller, modern army is a stronger one.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_cocom_relaxation: Since 1949 the Western Coordinating Committee for Multilateral Export Controls, CoCom, has kept advanced technology out of Soviet hands. The Directorate offers Washington a bargain: closer economic cooperation, scientific exchange and political predictability in return for easing the embargo lists on computers and electronics. Whether the Americans accept depends on how far they trust the new men in Moscow.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_the_future_of_the_directo: The Directorate has transformed the Union, but its rule rests on no mandate other than competence. Some systems men want to make their rule permanent and institutionalise technocratic government; others believe the modern society they have created now needs a parliament, elections and the rule of law. The Directorate must decide whether it is a transition or a destination.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_the_permanent_directorate: The systems men decide that their rule is not a transition. The Directorate becomes a permanent institution of state, its members co-opted on the basis of qualifications and its decisions binding on every ministry. Parliament and parties remain decorative. The Union becomes a managed society in which experts govern, and the citizen's role is to work, consume and trust the system.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_hand_over_to_parliament: The Directorate concludes that its historic task has been fulfilled. A modern economy and an educated society, its members reason, can no longer be governed from closed offices. Free elections are called, the Supreme Soviet is transformed into a real parliament and power is handed to the liberals of the Committee for Human Rights. The technocrats step back, hoping their reforms will outlive their rule.
COLDWAR_SOV_sd_the_managed_union: Gvishiani's dream has come true: the Soviet Union is governed as one great system, its economy steered by data, models and professional managers. Productivity and science flourish, and the Union has become a respected partner of the West in technology and trade. Whether this managed union is still socialism, or something altogether new, is a question its leaders no longer find important.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_the_solidarists_return: For forty years the People's Labour Union, the NTS, worked from exile, first in Belgrade and later in Frankfurt, where its Posev publishing house smuggled books and leaflets into the Union. Now the Solidarists return home, not as a hunted underground but as a governing party. Their doctrine of solidarism promises a third way between communism and capitalism, rooted in Russian tradition and Christian ethics.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_the_church_restored: Since Khrushchev's anti-religious campaign closed thousands of churches, the Russian Orthodox Church has survived as a tolerated but closely watched institution. The NTS restores its freedom: confiscated churches and monasteries are returned, seminaries reopen and the Patriarch of Moscow becomes a respected voice in public life. Some even speak openly of the House of Romanov again, a name that was taboo for half a century.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_private_property: Solidarism regards private property as the foundation of human dignity and responsibility. Small businesses, workshops, shops and service enterprises are returned to private hands, and citizens may once again own land, a house and the tools of their own trade. The nomenklatura, which controlled all property in the name of the people, loses the very basis of its power.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_the_model: The NTS leadership is divided over the economy. The old guard of the Solidarists wants an organic, corporate order in which employers, workers and the state cooperate through professional chambers. Younger members, inspired by the West German economic miracle, call for a genuine free market. The decision will shape the new Russia for generations.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_solidarist_corporatism: The Solidarists choose their original doctrine. Society is organised into professional corporations in which entrepreneurs, employees and the state negotiate wages, prices and working conditions together. Class struggle is to be replaced by solidarity, and the trade unions, freed from party control, become genuine partners rather than transmission belts. Critics fear the system is too slow and too comfortable for those already inside it.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_free_market_russia: The younger generation of the NTS prevails. Prices are freed, state enterprises are opened to competition and the ruble is set on the road towards convertibility. The model is Ludwig Erhard's West Germany, which rose from ruins within a single decade. The transition is painful and old certainties disappear, but the market promises a prosperity the plan never delivered.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_decollectivisation: The kolkhozy and sovkhozy were born of Stalin's war against the peasantry, and the NTS regards them as a crime that must be undone. Collective farms are dissolved, their land divided among the families who work it, and the peasant becomes a free farmer once more. The transition will be chaotic, but for the first time since 1929 the Russian village belongs to those who till its soil.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_the_constituent_assembly: In January 1918 the Bolsheviks dispersed the only freely elected Constituent Assembly in Russian history after a single session. The NTS now convenes a new one. Elected by universal suffrage, it is to give the country a constitution, decide the form of the state and settle the relationship between the peoples of the old Union. It is the long-delayed answer to 1918.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_into_the_west: The NTS has always seen Russia as part of Christian Europe, and its leaders spent decades in exile in the West. The new government breaks with the Eastern bloc and seeks a place alongside the Western democracies. In Bonn, where the NTS has long had friends, the decision is greeted with particular relief. The Cold War, at least as the world has known it, is coming to an end.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_the_republics_question: The Union was held together by the party and the army; without the communist monopoly, its fifteen republics face a fundamental question. Should the new Russia become a nation state that lets the other peoples go their own way, or can the old Union be transformed into a voluntary association of free nations? The answer will redraw the map of Eurasia.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_a_russian_federation: The NTS chooses Russia over empire. The new government offers every union republic the right to determine its own future, while Russia itself is reorganised as a democratic federation. In Kiev, Tbilisi, Vilnius and Tashkent the offer is received with astonishment, and in some places with jubilation. Russia becomes smaller, but it is no longer a prison of nations.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_a_union_of_nations: The NTS decides to keep the peoples of the old Union together, but on an entirely new basis. Instead of the dictatorship of a party, a voluntary association of equal nations is to emerge, with common defence, a common market and broad autonomy for each member. Not every republic is convinced, but many leaders see more advantages than dangers in remaining together.
COLDWAR_SOV_nts_the_new_russia: Half a century after the revolution, Russia has found its way back to itself. A free economy, a restored church and a government that grew out of the emigration have created a state the old exiles in Frankfurt and Paris could only dream of. The new Russia is a partner of the West, proud of its past and finally able to look to the future.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_the_committee_governs: In November 1970 Andrei Sakharov, Valery Chalidze and Andrei Tverdokhlebov founded the Committee for Human Rights in the USSR, a tiny circle of scientists defending the constitution against the state. Now this committee governs. Its programme rests on Sakharov's idea of convergence: socialism and capitalism must learn from each other, disarm and cooperate if humanity is to survive.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_release_the_prisoners: Thousands of Soviet citizens sit in labour camps and psychiatric hospitals for their opinions, their faith or their national aspirations. The new government opens the gates: political prisoners are amnestied, the special psychiatric hospitals are investigated and the Chronicle of Current Events can finally be published openly. The West applauds, while the KGB watches in disbelief as its opponents walk free.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_end_the_party_monopoly: For half a century the Communist Party has claimed the leading role in Soviet society without any vote ever confirming it. The Committee abolishes this monopoly: new parties may form, candidates may compete and the Supreme Soviet will be chosen in free and secret elections. The nomenklatura sees its world collapse, and many communists face the unaccustomed task of persuading voters.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_the_economic_question: Sakharov's convergence theory leaves an open question: how far should the economy move towards the market? Some members of the Committee want a mixed economy in which private and state enterprises compete as equals. Others prefer the West German or Scandinavian social market, where a strong welfare state cushions the effects of competition. Both camps agree that the old plan cannot continue unchanged.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_the_convergence_economy: The Committee chooses convergence in its purest form. State enterprises are given autonomy, private and cooperative businesses are legalised, and market prices take over where planning has failed. The economy becomes a hybrid of socialist and capitalist elements, just as Sakharov predicted in his 1968 essay. Supporters see the future of both systems; opponents see neither one thing nor the other.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_the_social_market: The Committee chooses the social market. Competition and private initiative are permitted, but within a strong framework of social security: guaranteed pensions, free healthcare, unemployment insurance and collective bargaining. The aim is to give Soviet citizens the freedom of the West without taking away the security they have grown accustomed to. It is expensive, but it keeps the country stable.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_the_rule_of_law: Valery Chalidze and his colleagues have always insisted that the Soviet constitution is a decent document that is simply never applied. The Committee now makes it binding: courts become independent, the procuracy is placed under legal control, and arbitrary arrests and telephone justice are forbidden. Officials discover, to their surprise, that the law applies to them as well.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_a_free_press: For decades the censors of Glavlit have shaped every newspaper, book and film in the Union. The Committee abolishes censorship. Samizdat authors publish openly, new newspapers appear and foreign radio stations are no longer jammed. The state loses its monopoly on truth, and with it much of its ability to steer public opinion, but science and culture flourish in the new freedom.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_disarmament: Sakharov, the father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, has long warned that the arms race threatens the survival of humanity. The Committee acts on his conviction: defence spending is cut drastically, divisions are disbanded and the Union declares itself ready to make unilateral gestures in nuclear disarmament. The generals are outraged, but the world takes notice of a superpower that disarms of its own accord.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_the_convergence_treaty: Convergence cannot be the work of one side alone. The Committee proposes a comprehensive treaty to Washington: mutual reductions in strategic arms, joint scientific programmes and a gradual opening of both societies to each other. It would be the greatest step towards lasting peace since 1945. Whether the United States is willing to take the outstretched hand remains to be seen.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_the_union_question: Since 1936 the Soviet constitution has guaranteed each union republic the right to secede, a right that was never meant to be used. The Committee, which takes the constitution at its word, must now decide whether to let the republics actually exercise it, or to keep them together in a reformed democratic federation. Neither choice will be easy, and both will be contested.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_the_right_of_secession: The Committee honours the constitution to the letter. Every union republic is free to hold a referendum and leave the Union if its people so wish. In the Baltic republics, the Caucasus and Ukraine, national movements prepare to vote. Moscow accepts that a Union held together by force cannot be a democratic one, even if this means the end of the old state.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_a_democratic_federation: The Committee seeks to preserve the Union on a democratic basis. A new treaty of union gives the republics broad self-government, their own freely elected parliaments and guaranteed rights for minorities, while foreign policy, defence and currency remain common. The hope is that peoples who suffered together under Stalin will choose to build a free federation together as well.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_join_the_free_world: Having embraced democracy, human rights and the rule of law, the new Soviet Union no longer sees any reason to stand against the West. The Committee leaves the logic of bloc confrontation behind and seeks partnership with the democratic world. For the first time since 1945, Moscow and Washington stand on the same side, and the Iron Curtain begins to lift.
COLDWAR_SOV_chr_the_open_society: The Soviet Union has become an open society, with free elections, a free press, independent courts and open borders. Sakharov's vision of convergence has become reality, and the country that once frightened the world is now among its most active partners in science and diplomacy. Many problems remain, but they are debated openly rather than hidden behind closed doors.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_socialist_democracy: Roy Medvedev, the historian whose manuscript 'Let History Judge' documented Stalin's crimes, has always believed that socialism and democracy belong together. His Union of Democratic Socialists now governs. It does not want to abolish socialism, but to free it from bureaucracy and dictatorship, in the spirit of the Prague Spring and the reform communists of Western Europe.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_multi_party_socialism: Medvedev's central demand is pluralism within socialism. New parties are allowed, provided they accept the socialist foundations of the constitution: social democrats, agrarians, Christian socialists and independent Marxists. The Communist Party must compete for votes like any other. Critics on the right call it a half-measure, while critics on the left call it the beginning of the end.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_the_rehabilitations: Medvedev's 'Let History Judge' becomes state policy. The archives are opened, the victims of the purges are rehabilitated by name, and the roles of Stalin, Beria and their accomplices are examined in public. Khrushchev's secret speech of 1956 was only a beginning; now the full truth is spoken. It is painful and unsettling, but the party believes that only honesty can restore its credibility.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_the_model: Democratic socialism can take many forms, and the government looks westwards for inspiration. Some favour the path of Luigi Longo and Enrico Berlinguer's Italian Communist Party, which combines Marxism with parliamentary democracy and independence from Moscow. Others prefer the Sweden of Olof Palme, a social democracy that has achieved prosperity and equality without revolution. The choice will shape the new Soviet socialism.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_eurocommunist_alliance: The government chooses Rome. Close ties are forged with the Italian and French Communist Parties, which have long sought a democratic road to socialism free of Moscow's tutelage. Together they form a new current within the world communist movement, one that respects elections, civil liberties and national paths. In Western Europe the Soviet Union suddenly appears as an ally of reform rather than its enemy.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_the_scandinavian_model: The government chooses Stockholm. Following the example of Olof Palme's Sweden, it builds a generous welfare state with comprehensive health insurance, housing programmes, decent pensions and equal opportunities in education. Market mechanisms are tolerated where they serve society, but social justice remains the goal. It is an expensive model, but it creates a broad base of satisfied citizens and social peace.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_workers_participation: Socialist democracy must not stop at the factory gates. Workers' councils are elected in every enterprise, with the right to take part in decisions on production, wages and the appointment of managers. The model draws on Yugoslav self-management and West German co-determination. Productivity rises as workers gain a real stake in their enterprises, and the trade unions rediscover their purpose.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_cut_the_defence_budget: The Soviet military absorbs resources that the economy and the consumer urgently need. The government cuts the defence budget, reduces conventional forces in Central Europe and redirects funds to housing, healthcare and consumer goods. The General Staff warns of weakness, but the government is convinced that the greatest threat to socialism is not NATO but the empty shelves of Soviet shops.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_detente_partners: Willy Brandt's new eastern policy and Olof Palme's active neutrality show that social democrats in the West are looking for partners in the East. The government offers Bonn and Stockholm a special relationship: political dialogue, trade agreements and cooperation between parties that share the goal of a democratic socialism. The Moscow Treaty of August 1970 could become the start of something much bigger.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_the_final_question: The reforms have transformed the Union, but one question remains open. Should socialism stay the fixed foundation of the state, with pluralism only within its boundaries, or should the people be free to choose any path, including a return to capitalism? Medvedev himself is a convinced socialist, but many in his party believe that democracy cannot be limited by any doctrine.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_socialism_remains: The government decides that democracy will remain socialist. The socialist foundations of the economy stay enshrined in the constitution, and parties that reject them are not admitted to elections. Within these boundaries, debate is free and lively. Supporters see this as the true fulfilment of Lenin's promise of soviet democracy; critics see a democracy with a safety catch.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_full_democracy: The government decides that democracy cannot have limits. All restrictions on parties are lifted, including on those that question socialism itself, and the people will decide in free elections which economic and political order they want. It is a bold gamble that could end with the voters rejecting the very socialism the reformers set out to save.
COLDWAR_SOV_uds_socialism_with_a_human_f: What Alexander Dubcek attempted in Prague in 1968, and what Soviet tanks crushed that August, has now come true in Moscow itself. Socialism has become democratic, open and humane, guided by the will of the people rather than the dictates of a bureaucracy. Eurocommunists in the West look on with admiration, and many in Eastern Europe dare to hope again.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_the_planners_govern: Nikolai Baibakov has led the State Planning Committee since 1965 and knows the Soviet economy better than any member of the Politburo. Now Gosplan itself takes power. The planners have no interest in ideological debates; they want balanced plans, reliable supply chains and efficient investment. The party's political role shrinks, and the country is run like a giant enterprise with Gosplan as its board of directors.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_ideology_retired: The technocrats have no use for slogans. Marxism-Leninism remains the official doctrine in textbooks and on banners, but it no longer guides decisions. Party secretaries lose their influence over economic questions, ideological commissions are reduced to ceremony and economic necessity becomes the only criterion. Many in the nomenklatura feel the ground slipping beneath their feet.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_the_material_balances: The method of material balances has been the backbone of Soviet planning since the 1930s: every ton of steel, every kilowatt and every machine must be matched between producers and consumers. Under the technocrats it is refined with computers, input-output tables and the linear programming of Leonid Kantorovich. Shortages and bottlenecks diminish as the plan finally becomes coherent.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_the_model: The planners must set a long-term strategy. One school wants to make the Union an engineering power that modernises its factories, invests in machine tools and competes on quality. The other wants to exploit the vast oil and gas fields of Western Siberia, discovered at Samotlor and Urengoy in the 1960s, and finance development through raw material exports. Both paths have their price.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_the_engineers_state: The planners choose the path of the engineers. Investment flows into machine building, instrument making, chemistry and electronics, and Soviet industry is equipped with modern machine tools and automated lines. The goal is an economy that lives not from the export of raw materials but from its own technical excellence. It is a long and expensive road, but it promises lasting independence.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_the_resource_state: The planners choose the path of resources. The oil fields of Western Siberia and the gas fields of the Far North are developed at full speed, pipelines are laid towards Europe and the hard currency they earn pays for imported machinery and grain. The gas-for-pipes agreement signed with West Germany in 1970 is only the beginning. The Union becomes an energy superpower, for better or worse.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_siberian_projects: The vast territories beyond the Urals hold the Union's future wealth, but they lack roads, railways and towns. The planners launch a series of great Siberian projects: new rail lines, hydroelectric plants on the Angara and Yenisei, and territorial production complexes that combine mining, energy and industry. The costs are enormous, but the planners think in decades rather than five-year plans.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_military_conversion: The military-industrial complex consumes the best engineers, materials and factories of the Union, while consumers wait years for a refrigerator. The planners order part of the defence industry converted to civilian production: tank plants turn out tractors, aircraft works build household appliances and missile designers work on consumer electronics. The arms lobby resists, and the transition proves harder than expected.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_trade_with_all: Ideology has no place in the planners' trade policy. The Union buys and sells wherever conditions are favourable, from West Germany and Japan to the Arab world and Latin America, and perhaps one day even China. Political considerations take a back seat to economic advantage. Foreign trade organisations gain greater autonomy, and Soviet goods appear in markets where they were never seen before.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_the_future: Gosplan's rule has brought order to the economy, but it rests on neither ideological nor democratic legitimacy. The planners must decide whether to make their rule permanent, as a government of experts without ideology, or to hand political power back to the party, which has kept its structures and members across the whole country. Either way, the planners intend to keep the plan.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_permanent_technocracy: The planners decide to stay. Gosplan becomes the supreme organ of state, the party is reduced to a mass organisation for mobilisation and education, and real power rests with economists, engineers and statisticians. The Union becomes a state without ideology, governed by figures and forecasts. It is efficient and stable, but its citizens have no voice in it.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_return_to_party_rule: The planners decide that their task is fulfilled. The economy has been put in order, and political leadership returns to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, which kept its structures and members throughout the technocratic interlude. The new party leadership inherits a stronger economy, and many planners return quietly to their offices in the Gosplan building on Marx Prospect.
COLDWAR_SOV_gt_the_planned_society: The planned society has become reality. Every factory, every city and every resource fits into a coherent system steered from Gosplan, and the old dream of a rationally organised economy has finally been realised. Shortages have become rare and growth steady. Whether this is still the socialism of Lenin or simply the triumph of the engineers is a question the planners do not care to debate.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_live_not_by_lies: Alexander Solzhenitsyn, Nobel laureate of 1970 and author of 'One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich', has always demanded one thing above all: never to take part in the lie. His followers now govern the country. Their programme is authoritarian and Orthodox, rejects Marxism as a foreign doctrine and places Russia's spiritual and national recovery above any global mission.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_letter_to_the_soviet_lea: In his Letter to the Soviet Leaders, Solzhenitsyn called on the Kremlin to abandon Marxist ideology, give up the empire, develop the Russian North-East and grant religious and cultural freedom. What was once an unanswered appeal from a persecuted writer is now the programme of government. The party is stripped of its ideological monopoly, and the nomenklatura loses its claim to rule.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_the_north_east: Solzhenitsyn believed that Russia's future lay not in foreign adventures but in its own vast and undeveloped North-East. The government turns towards Siberia and the Far East: new settlements, roads and railways open up the land, and its resources are developed carefully for the benefit of the Russian people rather than the arms race. A new frontier opens for a generation in search of purpose.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_the_form: Solzhenitsyn's followers agree that Russia needs an authoritarian but lawful government for the transition. Some want to build this order on the Orthodox Church as the moral foundation of state and society. Others want to revive the zemstvo, the local self-government created by the reforms of Alexander II, so that Russians learn to govern themselves from the bottom up. The choice will shape the new state.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_authoritarian_orthodoxy: The government chooses Orthodoxy as the foundation of the new order. The Church becomes the moral authority of the state, religious instruction returns to the schools and the government sees itself as the guardian of Russian spiritual tradition. Firm authority is justified as necessary for a people that must first recover from decades of lies. Dissent, now judged by religious rather than socialist standards, is still not welcome.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_the_zemstvo: The government chooses the zemstvo. Following the model of the 1864 reform, elected local assemblies take over responsibility for schools, roads, hospitals and agriculture in the districts and provinces. Moscow retains authority over the great questions of state, but Russians learn to manage their own affairs locally. The bureaucracy shrinks, and a modest civic life returns to the provinces.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_end_the_foreign_adventur: Solzhenitsyn argued that the Union was squandering its strength in Cuba, Vietnam, the Middle East and Eastern Europe while the Russian village decayed. The government ends this policy: aid to distant regimes is cut, military advisers are recalled and the satellites are told they must find their own way. Influence abroad declines, but resources are freed for Russia itself.
COLDWAR_SOV_lnl_the_village_restored: The writers of village prose, Valentin Rasputin, Vasily Belov and Vasily Shukshin, have mourned the dying Russian village for years. The government makes its revival a national priority: the Non-Black Earth Zone receives roads, schools and investment, collective farmers gain more freedom over their land, and young families are encouraged to return to the countryside. Russia seeks its roots in its own soil.
